title: Practice: expressions, functions and recursion
body: This is a set of original exercises for the "Basics" chapter of the CS 3110 textbook. They practise the same skills as that chapter without reproducing its exercises. Each exercise has a specification, and the program below contains one worked answer for each, with its output printed so you can check your own version against it.

Work in this order: read the specification, write your own solution without looking, run it on the examples, then compare with the worked answer. If they disagree, find the smallest input where they differ, because that input usually exposes a misread specification or a missing case.
Check the boundaries: century years for leap years, zero and single digits for digit sums, a zero remainder for gcd, and exponent zero for power.
challenge: Write `fib_pair n` returning the pair (fib n, fib (n+1)) in linear time with a single recursive call, and print `fst (fib_pair 30)`.
solution:
let rec fib_pair n = if n = 0 then (0, 1) else let a, b = fib_pair (n - 1) in (b, a + b)

let () = Printf.printf "%d\n" (fst (fib_pair 30))
question: Why does `power` halve the exponent?
correct: Squaring the half answer needs only about log2 e multiplications instead of e
wrong: It makes the function tail recursive
reasoning: Repeated squaring reuses the answer for e/2, so the work grows with the number of bits in e.

title: Practice: lists, variants, records and options
body: This is a set of original exercises for the "Data types" chapter of the CS 3110 textbook. They practise the same skills as that chapter without reproducing its exercises. Each exercise has a specification, and the program below contains one worked answer for each, with its output printed so you can check your own version against it.

Work in this order: read the specification, write your own solution without looking, run it on the examples, then compare with the worked answer. If they disagree, find the smallest input where they differ, because that input usually exposes a misread specification or a missing case.
Check the empty list, a list of one element and a list whose neighbours are all equal; each of compress, last_two and encode has a special case there.
code:
(* 1. last_two: the final two elements of a list, if there are at least two. *)
let rec last_two = function [] | [ _ ] -> None | [ a; b ] -> Some (a, b) | _ :: rest -> last_two rest

(* 2. compress: remove adjacent duplicates. *)
let rec compress = function a :: (b :: _ as rest) -> if a = b then compress rest else a :: compress rest | l -> l

(* 3. run-length encoding as (count, element) pairs. *)
let encode l =
  let rec go acc = function
    | [] -> List.rev acc
    | x :: rest -> (
        match acc with
        | (n, y) :: acc' when y = x -> go ((n + 1, y) :: acc') rest
        | _ -> go ((1, x) :: acc) rest)
  in
  go [] l

(* 4. a student record and its average, as an option for the empty case. *)
type student = { name : string; marks : int list }

let average s =
  match s.marks with [] -> None | ms -> Some (float_of_int (List.fold_left ( + ) 0 ms) /. float_of_int (List.length ms))

(* 5. a small expression type and its evaluator. *)
type shape = Circle of float | Rect of float * float | Square of float

let area = function Circle r -> 3.0 *. r *. r | Rect (w, h) -> w *. h | Square s -> s *. s

let () =
  (match last_two [ 1; 2; 3; 4 ] with Some (a, b) -> Printf.printf "%d %d\n" a b | None -> print_endline "none");
  print_endline (String.concat "," (List.map string_of_int (compress [ 1; 1; 2; 2; 2; 3; 1; 1 ])));
  print_endline (String.concat " " (List.map (fun (n, c) -> Printf.sprintf "%d%c" n c) (encode [ 'a'; 'a'; 'b'; 'c'; 'c'; 'c' ])));
  List.iter
    (fun s -> print_endline (match average s with Some a -> Printf.sprintf "%s %.1f" s.name a | None -> s.name ^ " none"))
    [ { name = "ada"; marks = [ 90; 80 ] }; { name = "bob"; marks = [] } ];
  Printf.printf "%.1f\n" (List.fold_left (fun acc s -> acc +. area s) 0.0 [ Circle 1.0; Rect (2.0, 3.0); Square 2.0 ])
challenge: Write `decode` that expands the run-length pairs back into a list, and print the decoded result of `encode ["x"; "x"; "y"]` joined by commas.
solution:
let encode l =
  let rec go acc = function
    | [] -> List.rev acc
    | x :: rest -> (
        match acc with
        | (n, y) :: acc' when y = x -> go ((n + 1, y) :: acc') rest
        | _ -> go ((1, x) :: acc) rest)
  in
  go [] l

let decode pairs = List.concat_map (fun (n, x) -> List.init n (fun _ -> x)) pairs

let () = print_endline (String.concat "," (decode (encode [ "x"; "x"; "y" ])))
question: Why does `average` return an option?
correct: The average of an empty list is undefined, and the type forces callers to handle that case
wrong: Because floats cannot be returned from a function
reasoning: An option makes the missing answer part of the type instead of an exception or a made-up value.

title: Practice: map, filter, fold and composition
body: This is a set of original exercises for the "Higher-order programming" chapter of the CS 3110 textbook. They practise the same skills as that chapter without reproducing its exercises. Each exercise has a specification, and the program below contains one worked answer for each, with its output printed so you can check your own version against it.

Work in this order: read the specification, write your own solution without looking, run it on the examples, then compare with the worked answer. If they disagree, find the smallest input where they differ, because that input usually exposes a misread specification or a missing case.
Check the direction of each fold: fold_left threads an accumulator from the left, fold_right rebuilds from the right, and swapping them reverses a list.
challenge: Define `compose_all fs` as a single function that applies a list of int functions right to left using `List.fold_right`, and print `compose_all [succ; (fun x -> x * 2)] 5`.
solution:
let compose_all fs = List.fold_right (fun f acc x -> f (acc x)) fs (fun x -> x)

let () = Printf.printf "%d\n" (compose_all [ succ; (fun x -> x * 2) ] 5)
question: Which fold builds a list in the same order as the input?
correct: fold_right with ::, because it processes the last element first and conses each earlier one on the front
wrong: Neither; folds always reverse a list
reasoning: fold_right visits from the end, so consing as it goes rebuilds the list in order; fold_left with :: reverses it.

title: Practice: signatures, abstraction and functors
body: This is a set of original exercises for the "Modules" chapter of the CS 3110 textbook. They practise the same skills as that chapter without reproducing its exercises. Each exercise has a specification, and the program below contains one worked answer for each, with its output printed so you can check your own version against it.

Work in this order: read the specification, write your own solution without looking, run it on the examples, then compare with the worked answer. If they disagree, find the smallest input where they differ, because that input usually exposes a misread specification or a missing case.
Check what the signature hides: a client must not be able to build a queue or look inside a set except through the exported functions.
code:
module type QUEUE = sig
  type 'a t

  val empty : 'a t
  val enqueue : 'a -> 'a t -> 'a t
  val dequeue : 'a t -> ('a * 'a t) option
  val size : 'a t -> int
end

module TwoListQueue : QUEUE = struct
  type 'a t = { front : 'a list; back : 'a list }

  let empty = { front = []; back = [] }
  let enqueue x q = { q with back = x :: q.back }

  let dequeue q =
    match q.front with
    | x :: front -> Some (x, { q with front })
    | [] -> (
        match List.rev q.back with [] -> None | x :: front -> Some (x, { front; back = [] }))

  let size q = List.length q.front + List.length q.back
end

(* A functor taking any ordered type and returning a sorted-unique set. *)
module type ORDERED = sig
  type t

  val compare : t -> t -> int
end

module MakeSortedSet (O : ORDERED) = struct
  type elt = O.t
  type t = elt list

  let empty = []

  let rec add x = function
    | [] -> [ x ]
    | y :: rest as l ->
        let c = O.compare x y in
        if c = 0 then l else if c < 0 then x :: l else y :: add x rest

  let to_list s = s
end

module IntSet = MakeSortedSet (Int)
module StringSet = MakeSortedSet (String)

let () =
  let q = TwoListQueue.(empty |> enqueue 1 |> enqueue 2 |> enqueue 3) in
  (match TwoListQueue.dequeue q with
   | Some (x, rest) -> Printf.printf "%d %d\n" x (TwoListQueue.size rest)
   | None -> print_endline "empty");
  print_endline (String.concat "," (List.map string_of_int (IntSet.to_list (List.fold_left (fun s x -> IntSet.add x s) IntSet.empty [ 3; 1; 2; 3; 1 ]))));
  print_endline (String.concat "," (StringSet.to_list (List.fold_left (fun s x -> StringSet.add x s) StringSet.empty [ "pear"; "apple"; "pear" ])))
challenge: Write a minimal queue module with `enqueue` and `peek`, hide its representation behind a signature, and print the peek of a queue holding 7 then 8.
solution:
module type QUEUE = sig
  type 'a t

  val empty : 'a t
  val enqueue : 'a -> 'a t -> 'a t
  val peek : 'a t -> 'a option
end

module Q : QUEUE = struct
  type 'a t = { front : 'a list; back : 'a list }

  let empty = { front = []; back = [] }
  let enqueue x q = { q with back = x :: q.back }

  let peek q =
    match q.front with x :: _ -> Some x | [] -> (match List.rev q.back with x :: _ -> Some x | [] -> None)
end

let () = match Q.(empty |> enqueue 7 |> enqueue 8 |> peek) with Some n -> Printf.printf "%d\n" n | None -> print_endline "empty"
question: What does the signature QUEUE hide from users of TwoListQueue?
correct: The representation of the queue type, so only the listed operations can build or inspect a queue
wrong: The fact that the queue exists
reasoning: The abstract type t lets the implementation change, for example to a tree, without breaking any client.

Check aliasing and independence: closures must not share state unless you meant them to, and in-place operations must handle empty and one-element arrays.
challenge: Write `swap_ends a` that exchanges the first and last elements of a non-empty array in place, and print the array [|1;2;3;4|] after calling it.
question: Why do two counters made by `make_counter ()` not interfere?
correct: Each call creates its own ref, and each closure captures a different one
wrong: Because refs are copied on every use
Because incr is atomic across closures
reasoning: The ref is allocated inside the function, so every call gets a fresh mutable cell.

title: Practice: monads, options and an event loop
body: This is a set of original exercises for the "Concurrency" chapter of the CS 3110 textbook. They practise the same skills as that chapter without reproducing its exercises. Each exercise has a specification, and the program below contains one worked answer for each, with its output printed so you can check your own version against it.

Work in this order: read the specification, write your own solution without looking, run it on the examples, then compare with the worked answer. If they disagree, find the smallest input where they differ, because that input usually exposes a misread specification or a missing case.
Check the failure path: a None must short-circuit the whole chain, and events scheduled for the same time must keep their scheduling order.
challenge: Write `both a b` for options that returns `Some (x, y)` only when both are `Some`, using `let*`, and print `both (Some 1) (Some "a")` formatted as "1,a".
solution:
let ( let* ) = Option.bind

let both a b =
  let* x = a in
  let* y = b in
  Some (x, y)

let () = match both (Some 1) (Some "a") with Some (x, y) -> Printf.printf "%d,%s\n" x y | None -> print_endline "none"
question: What does `let* x = e in body` do when `e` is `None` in the option monad?
correct: It skips the body and the whole expression is None
wrong: It runs the body with x set to a default
reasoning: bind on None returns None without calling the continuation, so a failure short-circuits the rest of the chain.

Check that your properties are not copies of the implementation, and that two properties together pin the behaviour down (order and length).
expectedStdout:
2 2 7
insert keeps order: true
insert adds one element: true
sorting twice is the same as once: true
a wrong claim, median is the mean: false
challenge: State the property "`median` of a list is between its minimum and maximum" and check it on 200 random non-empty lists, printing the result.
question: Why check that insertion returns a sorted list AND one element longer?
correct: A function can satisfy one property and still be wrong, for example by dropping an element
wrong: The two checks are the same property
Because sorted lists cannot change length
reasoning: Together the properties pin down the behaviour much more tightly than either one alone.

title: Practice: stacks, queues, trees and heaps
body: This is a set of original exercises for the "Data structures" chapter of the CS 3110 textbook. They practise the same skills as that chapter without reproducing its exercises. Each exercise has a specification, and the program below contains one worked answer for each, with its output printed so you can check your own version against it.

Work in this order: read the specification, write your own solution without looking, run it on the examples, then compare with the worked answer. If they disagree, find the smallest input where they differ, because that input usually exposes a misread specification or a missing case.
Check the invariant after every operation: a binary search tree stays ordered, and the two-stack queue pops in first-in first-out order.
challenge: Write `delete_min` for the binary search tree that returns the tree without its smallest element, and print the in-order list after removing the minimum of the tree built from [5;3;8;1].
solution:
type tree = Leaf | Node of tree * int * tree

let rec insert x = function
  | Leaf -> Node (Leaf, x, Leaf)
  | Node (l, v, r) as t -> if x < v then Node (insert x l, v, r) else if x > v then Node (l, v, insert x r) else t

let rec delete_min = function Leaf -> Leaf | Node (Leaf, _, r) -> r | Node (l, v, r) -> Node (delete_min l, v, r)
let rec inorder = function Leaf -> [] | Node (l, v, r) -> inorder l @ [ v ] @ inorder r

let () =
  let t = List.fold_left (fun t x -> insert x t) Leaf [ 5; 3; 8; 1 ] in
  print_endline (String.concat "," (List.map string_of_int (inorder (delete_min t))))
question: Why does the two-stack queue pop from the outbox first?
correct: The outbox already holds the oldest elements in order; only when it is empty is the inbox reversed
wrong: The outbox is faster to search
To avoid ever reversing a list
reasoning: Reversing the inbox only when the outbox runs dry moves each element once, which keeps the amortised cost constant.

title: Practice: extending a small interpreter
body: This is a set of original exercises for the "Interpreters" chapter of the CS 3110 textbook. They practise the same skills as that chapter without reproducing its exercises. Each exercise has a specification, and the program below contains one worked answer for each, with its output printed so you can check your own version against it.

Work in this order: read the specification, write your own solution without looking, run it on the examples, then compare with the worked answer. If they disagree, find the smallest input where they differ, because that input usually exposes a misread specification or a missing case.
Check evaluation order: the right side of a short-circuit operator must not run when the left side decides the answer, and unbound names must fail cleanly.
code:
type expr =
  | Int of int
  | Bool of bool
  | Var of string
  | Add of expr * expr
  | Le of expr * expr
  | Not of expr
  | And of expr * expr
  | If of expr * expr * expr
  | Let of string * expr * expr

type value = VInt of int | VBool of bool

let rec eval env = function
  | Int n -> VInt n
  | Bool b -> VBool b
  | Var x -> List.assoc x env
  | Add (a, b) -> (match (eval env a, eval env b) with VInt x, VInt y -> VInt (x + y) | _ -> failwith "type error")
  | Le (a, b) -> (match (eval env a, eval env b) with VInt x, VInt y -> VBool (x <= y) | _ -> failwith "type error")
  | Not e -> (match eval env e with VBool b -> VBool (not b) | _ -> failwith "type error")
  | And (a, b) -> (
      (* short-circuit: the right side is not evaluated when the left is false *)
      match eval env a with VBool false -> VBool false | VBool true -> eval env b | _ -> failwith "type error")
  | If (c, t, e) -> (match eval env c with VBool true -> eval env t | VBool false -> eval env e | _ -> failwith "type error")
  | Let (x, e1, e2) -> eval ((x, eval env e1) :: env) e2

let show = function VInt n -> string_of_int n | VBool b -> string_of_bool b

let () =
  let run e = try show (eval [] e) with Failure m -> m | Not_found -> "unbound" in
  print_endline (run (Let ("x", Int 5, If (Le (Var "x", Int 10), Add (Var "x", Int 1), Int 0))));
  print_endline (run (Not (Le (Int 3, Int 2))));
  print_endline (run (And (Bool false, Var "never_evaluated")));
  print_endline (run (And (Bool true, Bool true)));
  print_endline (run (Add (Int 1, Bool true)));
  print_endline (run (Var "y"))
expectedStdout:
6
true
false
true
type error
unbound
challenge: Write a tiny evaluator for booleans and variables with an `Or` constructor that short-circuits, and print the value of `Or (Bool true, Var "unused")`.
solution:
type expr = Bool of bool | Var of string | Or of expr * expr
type value = VBool of bool

let rec eval env = function
  | Bool b -> VBool b
  | Var x -> List.assoc x env
  | Or (a, b) -> (
      match eval env a with
      | VBool true -> VBool true
      | VBool false -> eval env b)

let () = match eval [] (Or (Bool true, Var "unused")) with VBool b -> Printf.printf "%b\n" b
question: Why must `And` evaluate its right operand only after checking the left?
correct: To short-circuit: if the left side is false the right side must not run, which matters for errors and effects
wrong: Because the right side is always a variable
reasoning: Short-circuit evaluation is part of the meaning of and/or, so the interpreter has to evaluate lazily on the right.
